name: No-sugar / sugar-free lifestyle

lead: A no-sugar lifestyle means avoiding added and free sugars, with the aim of clearer skin, slower skin ageing and a leaner body. It is a frequent theme in skincare and looksmaxxing talk.

For acne, the proposed chain is that high blood sugar and insulin raise IGF-1 and androgen activity, so lower sugar means fewer breakouts. Believers also point to glycation, where sugars bind to proteins such as collagen, as a route to ageing skin. Public health bodies recommend limiting free sugars, and Wikipedia reports dermatologists suggest a diet low in simple sugars for acne.

paras: People cut sweets, sugary drinks and sweetened foods, read labels for added sugar, and often replace them with whole foods. Skin changes are usually judged over weeks.
Cutting sugar is a mainstream dietary change. Extreme versions that remove whole food groups can affect nutrition.

chain: Lower glycation and blood sugar swings
angle.text: Users cut added sugar for clearer, younger-looking skin and a leaner body, through lower blood sugar swings and less glycation. Health guidelines support eating less sugar; skin-specific trials are thin.

lead: A no-sugar or sugar-free lifestyle is an eating pattern that removes or strongly limits added sugars, adopted by some people to improve skin, among other aims.

The WHO recommends reducing free sugars to under 10 percent of energy intake and suggests below 5 percent as a further target.[1] Wikipedia's acne article says dermatologists recommend a diet low in simple sugars to improve acne.[2]

paras: The WHO (2015) recommends limiting free sugars to under 10 percent of total energy and encourages under 5 percent.[1] The American Heart Association recommends 36 g a day for adult men and 25 g for women.[1]
Wikipedia states that eating fewer simple carbohydrates such as sugar may minimize acne and that dermatologists recommend a diet low in simple sugars.[2]
No studies found on sugar-free lifestyles for skin appearance in the sources reviewed. Studies of low-glycemic-load diets for acne are discussed in the article on low-glycemic diets.[2]

timeline.event: WHO publishes its guideline on sugars intake for adults and children.[1]
